newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters claims prize for backing NZ conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Peters claims prize for backing NZ conservatives.

text.p: Flamboyant Maori politician Winston Peters claimed the prize roles of treasurer and deputy prime minister on Tuesday in a New Zealand government coalition that keeps the conservative National Party in power.

Peters, relishing the drama of the moment, rejected an alternative pact with centre-left Labour as he announced his New Zealand First party's decision on live television after two months of tortuous negotiations.
"The New Zealand First caucus and executive have chosen this afternoon by a massive consensus to form a coalition government with the National Party until the next election in 1999," Peters declared.
The new treasurer wasted no time in renewing his calls for a lower currency and interest rates.

"There are some very real economic difficulties that need to be confronted with regard to an over-inflated Kiwi dollar and high interest rates that are affecting exporters and home-owners alike," he said.
Peters said the Reserve Bank Act, cornerstone of New Zealand's economic reforms, would be retained.
Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash promptly signed a new agreement widening the central bank's inflation target to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent, and adding a new goal of sustainable economic growth.
New Zealand First said tax cuts planned by National for July 1997 would be deferred by a year but would go ahead provided adequate budget surpluses were available.
The New Zealand dollar initially firmed to 71 U.S. cents on the news but retreated to around US$0.7020 in offshore trade as markets pondered how Peters would engineer a lower currency.
Economists said the central bank changes lent scope for interest rates to fall. One bank immediately cut mortgage rates.
The decision marked a huge about-turn for Peters, who berated National during the election campaign as an arrogant and callous party with no soul.
It represented a negotiating triumph for National's Prime Minister Jim Bolger, written off by some commentators on election night when a NZ First-Labour deal appeared more likely.

Political analysts said Peters faced a challenge to sell the deal to his supporters across New Zealand, including large numbers of Maoris who have historically favoured Labour but switched to NZ First in large numbers at the election.

"It's a victory for cynicism on an enormous scale...New Zealand First will reap a terrible payment. I don't think they will ever recover from this," left-wing political commentator Chris Trotter said.
"I think Winston Peters is dog meat," said Richard Prebble, leader of radical free-market Act New Zealand.
The charismatic Peters had kept the country waiting for nearly two months while he thrashed out secret deals with both National and Labour to put before his party.
Bolger said financial markets should be "totally calm" with the policies of the new government.
NZ First fought the election on an economic strategy of export-led growth and promises to put ordinary New Zealanders' interests above those of foreigners and big business.
National has 44 seats in the new 120-member parliament and Labour 37, with New Zealand First on 17.
